claims.text: High-entropy nanoparticles containing five or more metals in near-equal ratios can initially form a homogeneous solid solution.
Maintenance of a homogeneous solid solution is governed by the balance between sluggish atomic diffusion and thermally activated surface segregation.
High configurational entropy and uniformly distributed bond energies impart sluggish atomic diffusion.
High diffusion barriers allow the nanoparticles to remain structurally intact and chemically uniform at elevated temperatures.
Elements with lower diffusion barriers or lower cohesive energies segregate above a critical temperature.
Segregating elements may oxidize and thereby compromise nanoparticle stability and functional properties.
Average particle size or minor compositional tuning can be used to alter effective atomic diffusion characteristics.
The rate of thermally activated atomic diffusion dictates the onset or suppression of surface segregation and phase separation.
At lower temperatures, configurational entropy and associated diffusion barriers preserve the solid-solution state.
Increasing temperature enables thermally activated diffusion to overcome element-specific diffusion barriers.
Elements with lower cohesive energies are particularly prone to surface segregation.
Surface segregation can produce local phase decomposition or oxide formation.
Changes in surface or bulk composition perturb catalytic active sites or electron scattering and thereby modify functional performance.
Nanoparticles with higher diffusion barriers will retain a homogeneous single-phase structure and stable catalytic or thermoelectric performance over the tested temperature range.
Nanoparticles with lower effective diffusion barriers will exhibit detectable surface segregation and incipient phase decomposition near or above approximately 1400 K.
Segregation or phase decomposition will cause measurable changes in catalytic rate, electrical conductivity, or Seebeck coefficient relative to the as-synthesized baseline.
The proposed mechanism applies primarily to near-equiatomic nanoparticles smaller than 50 nm when heating does not cause complete melting or sintering.
